newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir leader urges Britain not to interfere.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir leader urges Britain not to interfere.

text.p: The chief of India's Jammu and Kashmir state on Monday urged Britain's new Labour government to ignore Kashmiri separatists' pleas and not meddle in the half-century-old regional conflict dividing India and Pakistan.

Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Farooq Abdullah said he hoped Britain's new prime minister, Tony Blair, would concentrate on solving his nation's own "problems", including strife in Northern Ireland, and not interfere in Kashmir.
"I think now time has come when India and Pakistan should heal their own wounds without interference from any other country of the world," Abdullah told a news conference in the Indian capital.
Indian officials have privately expressed fears over the Labour party's stance on Kashmir.
Blair was recently quoted by Indian media as saying his government would seek to help negotiate an agreement on Kashmir between India and Pakistan.

The Labour leader, who assumed power last week, told a regional Indian newspaper during the election campaign that Britain, as the former imperial power in India, must accept its responsibility in a dispute stretching back 50 years.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947, two of them over Kashmir. Labour was in power in Britain when the subcontinent was partitioned.

India says the issue can be discussed only bilaterally with Pakistan, without the involvement of a third party. Pakistan wants an internationally supervised referendum of Kashmiris and says outside help would be welcome to help resolve the dispute.
Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have been killed in the Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir since 1990 when simmering discontent with Indian rule erupted into an armed rebellion.
The leader of the separatist Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF) urged Blair to press India to accept a plebiscite.

"We hope that the new British government led by Tony Blair will intervene and use his good offices to settle the longstanding problem of Kashmir in accordance with the wishes of the people of Jammu and Kashmir," JKLF chairman Yasin Malik said in a statement on Sunday.
Malik said the new British foreign secretary, Robin Cook, had made a promise to separatists during a visit to Kashmir last year.

"He assured us of Labour Party's help and intervention if it came to power," Malik told Reuters in the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir, Srinagar, adding that the JKLF had supported Labour candidates in some regions of Britain.
But Abdullah urged Blair to "try and solve the Northern Ireland problem, which has been their problem for many years."
The Kashmir leader said he expected Blair to try to win over Britons who remain sceptical about a single European currency, and then look to help developing countries.

"What I would really require from the British government would be a tremendous amount of economic assistance," Abdullah said, citing efforts to clean up Srinagar's famed Dal Lake and replenish the region's forest cover.
"I hope that (Blair's) government would come forth in giving us some form of assistance in getting out of poverty," he said.
